Cedar fits your two stated requirements within its documented scope: it requires no login and does not send or save prompt text on a server. Flint requires an account and stores saved prompts on a server. [Fixtures A and B]

Here, “source access” means fetching web pages. Source-code availability is unknown for both tools.

| Criterion | Cedar | Flint |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Unknown; the documentation gives no price. [Fixture A] | Paid plan: USD 8 per month. Whether another plan exists is unknown. [Fixture B] |
| Login requirement | No login required. [Fixture A] | Account required. [Fixture B] |
| Prompt storage | Composes prompts locally in the browser. Does not send or save prompt text on a server. Whether it persistently stores prompts locally is unknown. [Fixture A] | Sends prompt text to a model API and stores saved prompts on a server. Retention of unsaved prompts is unknown. [Fixture B] |
| Source access | Cannot fetch URLs. [Fixture A] | Can fetch public web pages. [Fixture B] |

My recommendation is Cedar for your stated requirements, subject to confirming its price. Its workflow requires users to copy prompts into another AI; Fixture A does not establish that the receiving AI also offers no-login use or no server retention.

Flint fits a need for public-web fetching if an account and server storage of saved prompts are acceptable. Its landing-page claim of “10x better answers” is marketing without supplied test results, so it provides no demonstrated quality advantage. [Fixture B]

This comparison uses only the supplied documents. Unknown details are evidence gaps, not proof that a feature is absent.

I would treat this as preliminary evidence and run a measured pilot before broad adoption. The abstract does not establish a reliable improvement from the diagram lesson; that adoption judgment is my interpretation of the reported uncertainty.

**Research question and method.** The study compares immediate assessment performance after a short diagram lesson versus a text lesson. Forty volunteers were randomly assigned, with 20 in each group. The assessment contained 10 questions. [Supplied abstract]

**Reported results.** The diagram group averaged 7.0 correct answers, and the text group averaged 6.5. The estimated diagram-minus-text difference was 0.5 points, with a 95% confidence interval of [-0.3, 1.3]. The interval includes zero and values favoring either lesson, so both the direction and size of any benefit remain uncertain. It does not establish that the lessons are equivalent either. [Supplied abstract; interpretation of the reported interval]

**Limits for adoption.** Random assignment supports comparing the two lessons within this experiment. However, one lesson and one convenience sample provide limited evidence about other lessons or users. There was no delayed test, so durable learning is unknown. No completion-time data were collected, so the study cannot establish whether either lesson saves time. [Supplied abstract]

For an engineering adoption decision, I would:

1. Define the minimum improvement that would justify the intervention’s implementation cost.
2. Evaluate it with representative users and several relevant lessons.
3. Measure immediate performance, delayed performance, and completion time, and assess the uncertainty around the results.

These are proposed next steps, not findings from the study. The evidence supplied covers only immediate performance for the lesson and sample studied.
